newsitem.title: PERU: No sign of new talks in Peru's two-month hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: No sign of new talks in Peru's two-month hostage crisis.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis entered its 63rd day on Tuesday with still no date for new talks aimed at freeing the 72 hostages held at the Japanese ambassador's home by Marxist guerrillas of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
"We still don't have a date set for this week but they are going to continue," President Alberto Fujimori told reporters during a visit to the Amazon jungle on Monday.

Frustration at the apparent stalling of talks to pave the way for negotiations to end to the siege, now the longest in Latin American history, has given rise to speculation Fujimori will send in commandos to retake the residence by force.

Fujimori, whose own brother is among the hostages, denied reports he was planning a "violent entry", but an intelligence memorandum leaked to the media has revealed details of a plan to drop U.S. and Peruvian commandos into the compound on a moonless night and secure the building in just seven minutes.

The military option would have a high cost, with casualties expected to include three-quarters of the hostages, most of the rebels and about 20 commandos. "It is recommended that military action be left as a last resort," the army report said.

Fujimori has been urged by Japan to avoid bloodshed and reiterated Monday "we do not discard the possibility of a forceful intervention in the case that we have already explained" - that is, if any of the hostages are harmed.
The MRTA's captives include two cabinet ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, top security and court officials and Peruvian and Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
They were among the more than 500 guests seized by about 15 MRTA fighters who stormed a cocktail party at the residence Dec. 17. The others were freed soon after the attack.

Fujimori said he was "optimistic about finding a peaceful solution" through talks that have been held at a Red Cross safe house between MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini's lieutenant Rolly Rojas and the government's negotiator Domingo Palermo.

Vatican mediator Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, who made one of his regular visits to the residence Monday, said he and guarantors from Canada and the Red Cross were merely working on proposals "to enable the continuation of the conversations."
The MRTA's main demand, that 400 jailed comrades be freed, is totally rejected by Fujimori.

Hostages' families and sympathisers marked Monday the two- month anniversary of the siege, which now beats the 61-day siege of the Dominican Republic's embassy in Bogota by M-19 guerrillas, previously Latin America's longest hostage crisis.

A Peruvian mothers' grouup marched outside the residence singing "We Want Peace" and holding white roses "symbolizing the beauty of human life and importance of the lives of all those inside the residence."

Hostages' families sent their love to the 72 men over local radio. One story that has warmed the heart of the public is that of the 12-year-old son of a judge who wrote to Japanese Prime Miniser Ryutaro Hashimoto asking to help free his father.
Ryutaro's reply, asking little Hugo Sivina to "pray a lot and have faith", was read out on local radio.

Worries about the health of the most middle-aged hostages are increasing as the days go by, with Peruvian Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer warning Monday that health emergencies could happen "at any moment". Aid workers say captives are suffering hypertension, digestive problems, asthma and depression.

Elsewhere in Peru the guerrilla war that has cost 30,000 lives in 17 years continued with the killing of two state road workers in the Ayacucho highlands by about 20 suspected members of the Shining Path, the MRTA's larger Maoist rival.
